Banking and card acquiring in Cyprus

What a new business meets on the way from incorporation to its first card payment: the documents at each stage, the contracts it signs, who may serve it, which acts and bodies govern each step, what it pays in tax and fees, and how all of that moved between 2013 and 2026. Two sections follow a founder who lives in Cyprus and is not a citizen: what the residence status allows and what he registers himself.

Reference study, not legal or tax advice. Every statement carries its status as of 4 or 5 October 2026 and a number that leads to the record behind it and to the document that record was read in. Prices, product availability and statements that something is not published hold for that date only; the last section lists what was not established and when to look again.

gid research rounds cyprus-banking-acquiring, cyprus-banking-gaps and cyprus-founder-path · 4–5 October 2026 · 879 records in memory, 87.9% read in the primary document · seventeen research slices, each checked by two adversarial verifiers: 478 of 748 facts corrected, none refuted · the page was written from the memory records and every item was checked against them

  1. Question 1A company is formed through an advocate; tax registration is due in 60 days, owner filing in 90In outline, as of 4 October 2026: name approval; incorporation with an advocate-drafted memorandum and articles; Tax Register within 60 days; beneficial-owner register within 90 days; bank account; card contract. A sole trader forms no company; with a place of business in Cyprus he registers a business name unless he trades under his own true name.
  2. Question 1, continuedIncorporation asks for no residence document; the tax-number and CY Login pages ask for oneOn 5 October 2026 the Registrar identifies a founder by document number, not immigration status; the tax-number and CY Login pages ask for a registration certificate or residence permit. For social insurance a shareholder working in his private company is an employed person. A third-country national's work there turns on the permit; there the documents stop.
  3. Question 1, continuedUnion citizens: work is a ground of residence by Law; third-country nationals: the permit decidesRead 5 October 2026: for a citizen of another EU or EEA state work is a ground of residence, and the registration certificate is a duty, not a precondition. For a third-country national the permit decides: a visitor-permit holder may not work or do business without the Director's prior written permission; the Startup Visa is stated valid until December 2026.
  4. Question 2Two contracts: bank terms that waive statutory protections, merchant terms mostly under foreign lawA company that is not a micro-enterprise may waive parts of Law 31(I)/2018, and the three large banks' terms do it: at Bank of Cyprus amendments, fee increases included, need no prior notice; at all three a payment must be disputed in two months or less. Merchant terms are under Irish, Lithuanian, Greek, Dutch or Luxembourg law, JCC's under Cyprus law.
  5. Question 2, continuedBank carve-outs for larger businesses predate 2018; foreign providers moved contracts into the EUBank of Cyprus's 2011 edition and Hellenic Bank's 2017 edition withheld the two months' notice from companies that are not micro-enterprises. Dated fee tables show new and higher account charges and, in 2020-2022, charges on euro balances. Between 2019 and 2022 four foreign providers moved their Cyprus contracts out of United Kingdom entities or English law.
  6. Question 3Entry points: banks hold the accounts; resident card acquirers are payment and e-money institutionsOn 4 October 2026 the Central Bank of Cyprus (CBC) register lists four locally authorised credit institutions and three subsidiaries of EU banks. Among resident providers, per a CBC release, only payment and e-money institutions acquire cards; eleven Cyprus-licensed firms, JCC among them, offer it on their sites. Others, banks too, serve Cyprus cross-border.
  7. Question 3, continuedThe market in numbers, 2012-2026: fewer banks, more payment firms, volumes mostly abroadRegister entries of credit institutions fell from 57 (November 2015) to 18 (June 2025). Official totals of payment and e-money institutions disagree. Cyprus-resident providers acquired 1,576 million card payments in 2025 (second half provisional), 77% at points of sale abroad. Non-residents' share of deposits fell from 38.3% in 2012 to 11.9% in August 2026.
  8. Question 4Online shop: online contract and published prices. Café: a card duty and JCC's unpublished priceBoth walk-throughs are outlines assembled from records. Selling online as such needs no licence; the shop accepts Stripe's agreement online. The café needs a catering licence, unless excluded, and municipal licences inside a municipality, must accept cards under a 2021 decree and chooses JCC's individually priced agreement or a provider's published tariff.
  9. Question 5The Central Bank supervises providers; merchants' card duties sit with tax and consumer bodiesThe Central Bank of Cyprus supervises credit, payment and e-money institutions and is their anti-money-laundering (AML) supervisor; the European Central Bank supervises significant banks prudentially. The Tax Department enforces the card-acceptance duty, the Consumer Protection Service the surcharge rules. Card schemes set an acquirer's checks on a merchant.
  10. Question 5, continuedWhat Visa, Mastercard and PCI ask: registration, thresholds, disputes, questionnaires, interchangeThe schemes bind the acquirer, which passes the duties on by contract. Visa prints its high-risk categories and monitoring thresholds; Mastercard stopped printing its chargeback thresholds by 2021. Interchange is 0.20% and 0.30% on EEA consumer cards and mostly 1.3% to 2.0% on commercial cards; neither scheme's European fee page publishes scheme fees.
  11. Question 6From 2026: 15% corporate tax, 5% defence contribution on dividends, no stamp dutyThe reform in force since 1 January 2026 raised corporate income tax from 12.5% to 15%, cut the special defence contribution (SDC) on dividends to 5% for resident, domiciled individuals, with a 17% transitional rule, and repealed stamp duty. A company pays corporate tax and payroll contributions; a sole trader the personal scale and 16.6% social insurance.
  12. Question 7KYC: the law says what must be established, each institution publishes its own list or noneLaw 188(I)/2007 requires the identity of the customer and the beneficial owner to be verified before a business relationship starts, with derogations. The Central Bank of Cyprus directive in force since 2 June 2025 fixes the data and documents for a person and a company. Published lists differ: some 'ask for', some say 'may be requested', some publish none.
  13. Question 7, continuedNon-resident owners: one directive for all, separate bank price lists, country lists and sanctionsThe Central Bank of Cyprus (CBC) directive of 2025 has no separate regime for non-resident customers. What differs sits around it: the three large banks' price lists for international clients, the EU list of high-risk third countries (26 jurisdictions on 4 October 2026, Russia since 29 January 2026) and the EU sanctions on Russian and Belarusian clients.
  14. Question 8The Registrar charges €165 to register a company; an advocate and a statutory auditor are requiredAs of 4 Oct 2026 the Registrar charges €165 to register a company with share capital; the advocates' stamp is €40 for capital up to €2,000. An advocate must draft the memorandum and articles; a statutory auditor must audit or review the accounts. Review limits: €300,000 net turnover (per ICPAC, periods beginning from 6 February 2026), €500,000 total assets.
  15. 2013–20262013 to 2026 and the dates already fixed: what circulates is often not the date of effectTwo session notes describe one pattern: the date in circulation - an announcement, a vote, a Gazette date, a recommendation - is often not the date of effect. Events carry the date of effect where a record gives one; the text says which. Entries after 5 October 2026 are dates fixed in or derived from adopted acts, scheme rules, notices or official pages.
  16. Not establishedWhat this round did not establish, and which statements will go staleQuestions the records leave open or only narrow, and negatives true on 4 or 5 October 2026 that need another look: prices, product availability, 'not published' statements, pending EU law, transitional tax rules and points the texts read leave open for a non-citizen founder. Each item says what is established, where it was looked for and what would close it.
Question 1 · Documents by stage

A company is formed through an advocate; tax registration is due in 60 days, owner filing in 90

In outline, as of 4 October 2026: name approval; incorporation with an advocate-drafted memorandum and articles; Tax Register within 60 days; beneficial-owner register within 90 days; bank account; card contract. A sole trader forms no company; with a place of business in Cyprus he registers a business name unless he trades under his own true name.

  2. 2Namebefore incorporation
  3. 3Incorporationafter approval of the name
  4. 4Tax Registerwithin 60 days of incorporation

  6. 6Employer registrationno later than one day before the day it expects to become an employer

A new private company, stage by stage (as of 4 October 2026)

  1. Formbefore anything is filed
    A natural person may trade without forming a company; the Registrar's table sets 'unlimited liability of the owner of a business name' against 'limited liability of company members'. Private companies have no minimum share capital (Registrar). From tax year 2026 an individual in business with annual turnover and other gross income up to €120,000 (before: €70,000) is exempt from preparing the accounts that must be audited or reviewed (Law 4/1978, art. 30).123
  2. Namebefore incorporation
    Each proposed name goes to the Registrar of Companies for approval. An approved name stays reserved for six months, within which the incorporation application must be filed. On 5 October 2026 the Registrar's page 'Obtain access to e-filing' says a user first registers on the gateway 'gov.cy' (the links lead to CY Login) and can then submit, among others, the name-approval application and the registration of a company; it names no nationality or residence condition and does not say the profile must be verified.45
  3. Incorporationafter approval of the name
    Only a practising advocate may draft the memorandum and articles (Advocates Law, s. 11(5)). By hand or post: form HE1 (statutory declaration sworn before the court by the entrusted lawyer), HE2 (registered office), HE3 (first directors and secretary) and the memorandum and articles signed in Greek; where applicable, the competent authority's consent or pre-approval for restricted words or a regulated nature of business. E-filing: HE1, memorandum and articles and a solemn declaration of the witness of signatures.67
  4. Tax Registerwithin 60 days of incorporation
    The company gives notice for registration and obtains a tax identification number (Law 4/1978, s. 5A(2), as worded from 1 January 2026). Per the Tax Department (announcement of 9 April 2026; page read 5 Oct 2026), from 1 July 2026 the request is made only when the Tax For All portal is entered through CY Login; whose profile, the announcement does not say. Attached: certificates of incorporation, registered office, directors and secretary, and shareholders, and the submitting officer's identification document.8910
  5. VATwhen a registration trigger is met, or before any sale on intention
    Triggers on the Tax Department's page: taxable supplies above €15,600 in the 12 months to any month-end, or reasonable grounds to expect that within 30 days; no threshold for services to taxable persons in another Member State where the recipient accounts for the VAT. Form T.F. 1101 goes on paper to a District Office with the Registrar's certificates and evidence of economic activity or of the obligation or right to register. On whether a tax number must come first, the form and the Department's page differ.11121314
  6. Employer registrationno later than one day before the day it expects to become an employer
    An employer applies to register with the Social Insurance Services no later than one day before it expects to become one, on form YKA 1-001 with, per the Services' page (23.03.2021), the Registrar's certificates of incorporation, directors and secretary, and shareholders. Each hiring is notified no later than one day before it, only electronically (Social Insurance (Contributions) Regulations, regs 3(2) and 5, as replaced by K.D.P. 167/2017, in force 13 September 2021); the channel, Ergani, is not named in them.1516171819
  7. Beneficial-owner registerwithin 90 days of incorporation
    The company files its beneficial-owner (UBO) details in the Registrar's electronic register (Directive K.D.P. 112/2021, para. 9(1); K.D.P. is the Cyprus numbering for regulatory administrative acts); no documents or fees are submitted. Per the Registrar's guidance only the entity's own officer or partner may submit them, not a person acting on its behalf such as a service provider.202122
  8. Bank accountafter incorporation
    A bank that starts a relationship with a company obliged to register its beneficial owners must collect proof of that registration or an extract from the register (Law 188(I)/2007, art. 62(1) proviso). On 4 October 2026 Bank of Cyprus served two versions of its 'Limited Company Account' checklist and states no version date; both ask for the Beneficial Owners Register registration receipt, and they differ on whether the Registrar of Companies documents are submitted at the start or may be requested later.23242526
  9. Card-acceptance contractwithin one month of starting, where the main activity code is listed
    JCC's merchant application form (read 4 October 2026) states that a current bank account is mandatory. The card-acceptance duty falls on payees whose main activity code is in the Annex to Decree K.D.P. 259/2021, widened by three amending decrees in 2021 and 2022; a business that starts a listed activity after the initial deadline has one month from the start or the change to comply.27282930

A sole trader files instead

  • A business name (form EE1 or e-filing) within one month of commencing business, if he has a place of business in Cyprus and trades under a name that is not his true surname without any addition other than his true first names or initials (Partnerships and Business Names Law, Cap. 116, ss. 50(b), 52(1)).1
  • Registration with the Social Insurance Services and the Tax Department; a self-employed person applies to the Services no later than the day he starts work (Contributions Regulations as replaced by K.D.P. 167/2017, in force 13 September 2021). The Services' forms list (read 4 October 2026) carries YKA 1-008 and YKA 1-013, the government business portal names only YKA 1-008.3132

As read on 4 October 2026 the Social Insurance Services' pages still describe the paper hiring declaration, although since 13 September 2021 the declaration is submitted only electronically; the Services' page naming form YKA 1-001 was last updated on 23.03.2021. The government business portal (modified 12.08.2024) states the electronic notification through the Ergani system; its English calls the abolished 'certificate of commencement of employment' a 'Declaration for the recruitment'.1517

Source trap

Section 17(2) of the Companies Law also lets a person named in the articles as director or secretary make the declaration of compliance, but form HE1 as published by the Registrar on 4 October 2026 contains only an advocate's oath. The single HE1 without form HE3 of K.D.P. 368/2018 takes effect only by the Registrar's Gazette notification: the three found (K.D.P. 34/2021, 484/2021, 495/2021) bring in other forms, none names HE1, HE2, HE4 or HE32, and cylaw's index lists no further one up to 25 September 2026.686970

Open look again by 5 Apr 2027

K.D.P. 282/2025, 'the Companies Order of 2025' (Gazette No. 5969, 19.9.2025), lists HE1 as 'Formation of a company' and no HE3; it enters into force on a date fixed by a notification of the Registrar, and as of 4 Oct 2026 none appears in cylaw's index (to 25.9.2026) or on the Registrar's site. Its certificates will be issued through the Registrar's new electronic system, whose go-live slipped over five official statements from 'the 1st half of 2025' (12 October 2022) to 'the first quarter of 2027' (19 June 2026).7172

Open look again by 31 Dec 2026

Overdue filings carry a dated extension. On 4 September 2026 the Registrar announced that, following reminder letters sent on 9 February 2026 about overdue annual returns and the corresponding financial statements, their filing is extended until 31 December 2026; after that date the strike-off procedure under s. 327 of the Companies Law will continue for companies that have not complied. This is a separate track from the strike-off for unpaid annual levy announced on 30 September 2026.7374

Source trap

The Directive's access rule is out of date. Para. 12(1)(γ) of K.D.P. 112/2021, never amended, still gives 'any member of the wider public' access for €3.50 per entity; the Registrar suspended it by announcement from 23 November 2022, and Law 25(I)/2026 (20 March 2026) replaced public access in Law 188(I)/2007 with a legitimate-interest test. As of 4 Oct 2026 the Registrar publishes two routes, both for obliged entities only (€3.50 per entity), and no form, fee or procedure for a legitimate-interest request.757677

Provisional tax is a further yearly duty. A person with income other than emoluments submits its own estimate of the year's chargeable income before 31 July of the tax year (Law 4/1978, art. 24) and pays in two instalments, which the Tax Department's 2026 calendar dates 31 July and 31 December; the estimate can be revised until 31 December. A company formed after 30 June files its estimate by 31 December (proviso added by Law 243(I)/2025); one incorporated in October 2026 pays the provisional tax for 2026 in one instalment by 31 December 2026 (s. 38(1)(γ), proviso). Sections 24-26 do not address a company expecting no chargeable income.7879

Question 1, continued · A founder who lives in Cyprus and is not a citizen

Incorporation asks for no residence document; the tax-number and CY Login pages ask for one

On 5 October 2026 the Registrar identifies a founder by document number, not immigration status; the tax-number and CY Login pages ask for a registration certificate or residence permit. For social insurance a shareholder working in his private company is an employed person. A third-country national's work there turns on the permit; there the documents stop.

For everyone: the Registrar's review criteria (read 5 October 2026) identify a director or secretary by 'identity or passport number' and each shareholder by identity number and nationality, among other details; no residence permit, registration certificate or Cyprus address of the person is asked for. Being a non-Cypriot enters elsewhere: the Registrar's guidance opens the beneficial-owner register to a personal CY Login profile 'only for Cypriot citizens holding a Cypriot identity card'; the Ergani hire notice asks identifiers by nationality; the founder's own registrations ask for his certificate or permit; and, in outline, a third-country national's work there turns on the permit.363780818283

A citizen of another EU or EEA state: the order the documents set

  1. Registration certificatewithin four months of the date of arrival (Law 7(I)/2007, art. 10(1))
    A duty backed by a fine, not a legal precondition for economic activity where entitlement can be shown by other means (art. 23(1)). As read on 5 October 2026 the Tax Department's page and, for in-person identification, the CY Login help page nonetheless ask an EU citizen for it. In outline, his personal tax number needs only that certificate.3782848586
  2. The company registers as employerno later than one day before it expects to become an employer (Contributions Regulations, reg. 3(2))
    Form YKA 1-001 (edition 9/2021), handed in, per the Services' Employer Guide (PDF of 2 June 2025), at any District Social Insurance Office or at a Citizen Service Centre; for a director who is an alien the form takes an alien registration or passport number.164041
  3. Ergani account, then the hire notice for himselfno later than one day before the hiring (reg. 5(1))
    As of 5 October 2026 the account's registration form begins with the employer number, so the account comes second. Per the Ergani user manual (PDF of 7 September 2021), for a citizen of an EU state the notice takes an EU identity number with the country, an alien registration number and/or a social insurance number; if the match fails, the notice can go on once an identification file is uploaded.174381
  4. Social insurance numberwithin seven days of the hiring (reg. 4(2))
    The employer files form YKA 1-008 (edition 5/2019) at the nearest District Social Insurance Office for an employee not yet in the insured persons' register.3249
  5. Registration as a worker, if not yet registeredthe four months run from the date of arrival (art. 10(1))
    On the 'worker' ground form MEU1 (read 5 October 2026) asks his social insurance number and the Services' registration certificate, so social insurance registration comes first on that ground; the Department's list also asks a statement of contributions naming the last employer and salary. The Law asks, beside an identity card or passport, for the employer's confirmation of engagement or a certificate of employment (art. 10(4)(α)).84878889

A third-country national: the steps the documents carry, and where they stop

  1. The permit held
    In outline, what the texts regulate is activity, and it turns on the permit held (next section). The holder of a visitor's permit must not seek or accept employment, paid or unpaid, or carry on any business, trade or profession without the Director's prior written permission (Aliens and Immigration Regulations, reg. 14(3)).8390
  2. Shares and the office of director
    In outline: no approval to hold shares or to be entered as a director was found in the Companies Law or the immigration texts read on 5 October 2026. For a visitor no published text was found on whether an unpaid directorship is 'carrying on business' under reg. 14(3). Not established.8391
  3. Own tax number; CY Login profile
    As read on 5 October 2026 the Tax Department's page asks for the residence permit, all sides, without stating which kind (if only applied for: the payment receipt plus further documents); the CY Login help page asks, for in-person identification, for a residence permit showing the alien registration number and photograph (table below). In outline, the tax number needs only the permit.378286
  4. Work in the company: the documents stop
    In outline (texts read 5 October 2026): employment needs a permit naming the employer; running a business needs a status with free access to work, a Startup Visa (scheme stated valid until December 2026), an immigration permit in a self-employment category, or a Regulation 12 permit, which holders of visitor, student or employment permits may not apply for while in Cyprus. A company of foreign interests may employ third-country staff; no text read says whether its owner may be one.8392

The founder as employee of his own company (every nationality)

  • A shareholder who works for his private company is an employed person, not a self-employed one, whatever his nationality or the size of his shareholding (Social Insurance Law 59(I)/2010, First Schedule, Part I, para. 5).93
  • No minimum insurable earnings are fixed for him; contributions are due unless the earnings are negligible - below €2 a week or €7 a month (Law 59(I)/2010, s. 4; K.D.P. 289/2010, reg. 7).94
  • Minimum wage on 5 October 2026: €1,088 a month full-time, €979 before six months of continuous employment with the same employer (K.D.P. 350/2022 as amended by K.D.P. 427/2025). The Decree has no rule for directors or shareholders and does not address whether a sole shareholder-director is an 'employee'.9596
  • If he is its employee: the basic terms in writing within seven calendar days of the start, the rest within one month (Law 25(I)/2023, arts 11-12); no exception for directors is named.97

Question 1, continued · Residence status and what it allows

Union citizens: work is a ground of residence by Law; third-country nationals: the permit decides

Read 5 October 2026: for a citizen of another EU or EEA state work is a ground of residence, and the registration certificate is a duty, not a precondition. For a third-country national the permit decides: a visitor-permit holder may not work or do business without the Director's prior written permission; the Startup Visa is stated valid until December 2026.

Applications go to the Migration Department of the Deputy Ministry of Migration and International Protection; outside Nicosia district the district police Aliens and Immigration Unit serves by appointment, and eleven categories are examined only at the central offices in Nicosia (service instructions posted 19 December 2025). By the Department's notice of 11 March 2026, 'as of 2 April 2026, only the revised and updated versions of the forms will be accepted'.119120121

Company of foreign interests and Startup Visa: what the lists ask (third-country nationals), as read on 5 October 2026

  • Company of foreign interests, per the Business Facilitation Unit's page (modified 23 September 2026): a business meeting one of nine criteria, the first being majority ownership by third-country nationals ('50% plus'); where a third-country national owns 50% or less, that share must be worth at least €200,000, 'additional to the initial investment of €200.000'.151
  • The initial investment of €200,000 must have been made up to six months before the application and still be present: a deposit by the shareholders into the company's account at a credit institution licensed by the Central Bank (electronic money and payment institutions are not accepted), or the purchase of an office or equipment for business use.131
  • The company applies to the Unit only online, logged in with its own identified CY Login profile; Annex I asks, among others, for the beneficial-owner search certificate from the Registrar and a title deed or a lease of at least 12 months for business premises separate from any residence. No fee is stated.132
  • Startup Visa founder, per the Department's list (file uploaded 29 December 2025), among others: for paid employment a contract with a gross monthly salary of at least €850; for self-employment proof of at least €10,000 a year for living expenses and a ten-year bank guarantee for repatriation costs.152

The Startup Visa is stated 'valid until December 2026' (Guide dated December 2024, read 5 October 2026). Which length of the right applies, the Department's or the Guide's, is not settled by the two texts.92135

Source trap

Two dates for companies of foreign interests (texts read 5 October 2026). Each company commits to 30% Cypriot or EU staff within five years, counted per the Strategy text from the date it joined the scheme; the Department's page gives one date, 'after 2.1.2027, the ratio for new hires will be checked'. Holders of Key Personnel permits on a gross monthly salary of €2,000 or more may renew with the same employer without a pay rise only 'until 31.12.2026'.159

Source trap

Reading the Aliens and Immigration Law (Cap. 105): on 5 October 2026 the CyLaw consolidated text is one amendment behind. Its amendment history ends at Law 149(I)/2024, while Law 4(I)/2025 (Official Gazette No. 5026 of 14 February 2025) amends 49 of its sections. In the long-term-resident part only arts 18ΣΤ and 18Η(1Α)(β) change; arts 18Η(1), 18Θ, 18Ι and 18ΙΖ are not touched.160

Not established in this section

  • A visitor-permit holder as shareholder or unpaid director. Does an unpaid directorship or a passive shareholding of a third-country national on a visitor's permit count as 'employment, paid or unpaid' or as carrying on a business under Regulation 14(3), and how is the Director's prior written permission sought? look again by 5 Jan 2027
  • The Regulation 12 permit to exercise an independent profession. Is the permit of Regulation 12 of the Aliens and Immigration Regulations issued to third-country nationals at all in 2026, and on what form and criteria? look again by 5 Jan 2027
  • Startup Visa after December 2026. Does the Startup Visa continue after December 2026, and which duration of the founder's right applies now? look again by 5 Jan 2027

Question 2 · Agreements with the bank and with payment providers

Two contracts: bank terms that waive statutory protections, merchant terms mostly under foreign law

A company that is not a micro-enterprise may waive parts of Law 31(I)/2018, and the three large banks' terms do it: at Bank of Cyprus amendments, fee increases included, need no prior notice; at all three a payment must be disputed in two months or less. Merchant terms are under Irish, Lithuanian, Greek, Dutch or Luxembourg law, JCC's under Cyprus law.

The account

  • Only consumers have a right to an account: Law 64(I)/2017 makes credit institutions, unless exempted by the Central Bank, offer a basic payment account to consumers legally resident in the EU. A consumer is a natural person acting outside trade or profession; legal entities have no such right. Law 41(I)/2026 (Gazette, 2 April 2026) removed an account at another Cyprus credit institution as a ground for refusal.161162
  • A business account is priced by a dated fee table: Bank of Cyprus for legal entities (May 2026), Eurobank Limited (effective 16 September 2026), Alpha Bank Cyprus for individuals and small companies and for corporate and small medium companies (both valid from 6 April 2026). Each lists account maintenance and a review or assessment fee; the amounts: the table of bank clauses below and the last item of this list.163164165166
  • An institution must end the relationship if due diligence cannot be completed (Law 188(I)/2007, art. 62(4)). Since 2 June 2025 the Central Bank of Cyprus (CBC) Directive of 2025, para 12(7), requires obliged entities to ensure that their policies do not result in the general refusal or termination of relationships with entire categories of customers they regard as higher risk.167168
  • The other amounts (fee tables read 4 October 2026): Bank of Cyprus's 'file update / review fee' is EUR 100 for small to medium legal entities and EUR 250-750 for corporate group companies requiring enhanced due diligence; no line prices the opening of a company's first ordinary account. Eurobank: customer review, legal entities EUR 50. Alpha: small organisations EUR 12 a month per current account without a limit.163164165

Law 31(I)/2018 (in force since 18 April 2018; consolidated text read 4 October 2026): the framework contract and what a business may waive

  • Art. 38: where the payment service user is not a consumer, the parties may agree that Part III - transparency of conditions and information requirements - does not apply in whole or in part. A micro-enterprise, defined by arts 1 and 2(1) and (3) of the Annex to Recommendation 2003/361/EC and tested at the time the contract is concluded, is treated as a consumer and cannot contract out (art. 38(2)).169
  • Changes (art. 54): the provider proposes any change to the contract or the art. 52 information, charges included, at least two months before it is to apply; if the contract so provides, silence counts as acceptance and the user may terminate free of charge before that date. Interest or exchange rate changes that follow agreed reference rates may apply at once, without notice, if the contract says so (art. 54(3)).170
  • Ending the contract (art. 55): the user may terminate at any time unless a notice period of not more than one month is agreed, free of charge unless the contract has been in force for less than six months; the provider may terminate a contract of indefinite duration only if the contract so provides and with at least two months' notice on paper or another durable medium.171
  • Unauthorised payments, the default: the user notifies without undue delay and within 13 months of the debit date (art. 71(1)); the provider must prove authentication and accurate recording, and recorded use of an instrument is not necessarily sufficient proof of authorisation (art. 72); the payer may bear up to EUR 50 for a lost, stolen or misappropriated instrument (art. 74).172
  • What a business may waive (art. 61(1), as amended by Law 32(I)/2019): where the user is not a consumer the parties may agree that art. 62(1), art. 64(3)-(4), art. 72, art. 74, arts 76-77, art. 80 and arts 89-90 (liability for non-execution or defective execution) do not apply in whole or in part, and may agree time limits other than the 13 months of art. 71. Micro-enterprises are treated as consumers (art. 61(2)).173

What the schemes and the law require of the merchant agreement

  • Visa: an agreement with each merchant that obliges it to follow applicable law and the Visa Rules and not to submit illegal transactions, and reserves Visa's right to limit or terminate it (section 1.5.2.1, edition 18 April 2026).200
  • Mastercard (Mastercard Rules, edition 2 June 2026): a written agreement made directly by the acquirer, except for transactions acquired from its registered payment facilitator, with the substance of Rules 5.5 through 5.15; in the European Economic Area (EEA) also the merchant's duty to respond to cardholder disputes and handle chargebacks under the Chargeback Guide.201202
  • EU law: since 9 June 2016 the merchant service charge, interchange fee and scheme fees per category and brand of card, unless the merchant asks in writing for blended pricing (Regulation (EU) 2015/751, Article 9).203
  • Visa, Europe Region (section 10.17.1.1, edition 18 April 2026): the acquirer must also, unless law prohibits or specifies otherwise, warn the merchant in writing at the start that termination for cause may lead to a listing in the Visa Merchant Screening Service.204
  • Counterparty: Mastercard requires the acquirer itself to sign (Rule 7.6.1, edition 2 June 2026); Cyprus law lets payees contract for card acceptance only with payment service providers lawfully licensed within the meaning of Law 31(I)/2018 or their agents, unless legislation expressly provides otherwise (Law 4/1978, art. 30A(2), in force since 20 August 2020). That text does not mention payment facilitators.205206

Payment facilitator and sponsored merchant

  • Visa defines a payment facilitator as an entity that contracts with an acquirer on behalf of sponsored merchants (edition 18 April 2026); Mastercard requires the sponsored-merchant agreement to show that the facilitator enters into it on behalf of and as agent of the acquirer (Rule 7.8.1, edition 2 June 2026). Under both schemes the acquirer answers for the facilitator and its sponsored merchants.207208
  • Visa: a sponsored merchant that 'exceeds USD 1 million in annual Transaction volume', read as its own Visa volume, needs a direct agreement with the acquirer, before processing if new to the facilitator or within 2 years if existing; listed category codes and some relationships held 2 years with the same acquirer are exempt (section 5.3.1.4, edition 18 April 2026).209
  • Mastercard: above USD 10,000,000 in combined annual Mastercard and Maestro volume the sponsored merchant signs directly with a Mastercard licensee, unless a set of conditions all hold or its primary category code is on an exception list (Rule 7.8, edition 2 June 2026). Neither scheme has a Europe variation.209210
  • Stripe's Acquirer Disclosure, read 4 October 2026, names its own Irish electronic money institution (EMI) as acquirer for the EEA; the records infer that a Cyprus business at Stripe is a direct merchant, which the facilitator thresholds do not reach.211212
  • SumUp's Payment Terms say card-network rules may require some merchants, depending on payment volume, to sign a separate agreement with a partner institution or the networks (section 3). Revolut's terms give as an example a merchant processing 'at least USD$1m worth of American Express, Mastercard or Visa transactions annually', which may need a direct contract 'with a Payment Method Acquirer and us'.212213214

A House committee report of 23 May 2023 records the Ministry of Finance saying that 'the legislator's intention was the universal prohibition, without exceptions' of such charges; how the ban is enforced is told in the section on laws and supervisors.Law 31(I)/2018270271272

On 2 September 2019 the CBC said it intended to grant card issuers and acquirers that already supported a non-reusable, non-replicable element (e.g. OTP) for online card transactions 'a limited migration period', its length not yet determined by the European Banking Authority (EBA); the application date was not changed. The EBA Opinion of 16 October 2019 said migration plans should be completed by 31 December 2020, a recommendation on supervisory flexibility. On 24 December 2019 the CBC announced that it 'does not intend to take supervisory enforcement action against licensed institutions which have not implemented SCA in remote electronic card transactions by 31 December 2020, provided that these institutions have submitted a migration plan', and that 14 September 2019 'remains as the legal deadline'. Card-acceptance duty: later starters and the fine

  • A business that starts a listed activity after the initial deadline has one month from the start or the change to comply (K.D.P. 259/2021, paragraph 3(δ)).2829
  • A breach carries an administrative fine imposed by the Tax Commissioner under art. 50ΣΤ of Law 4/1978: up to EUR 2,000 as in force 20 February 2021, up to EUR 4,000 from 4 March 2022, up to EUR 6,000 from 1 January 2026. It is halved if paid within 30 days of notification and before any objection, or if a terminal purchase invoice is filed within 30 days of the complaint or inspection (art. 50ΣΤ(7)).289
  • The fine is not imposed if at the inspection the business shows a document certifying that a licensed payment service provider rejected its application for a terminal, or if it applied before the deadline and the terminal was not supplied for reasons attributable to the credit institution, certified in writing (art. 50ΣΤ(8), consolidated text read 4 October 2026).28

Question 2, continued · How the agreements changed, 2015–2026

Bank carve-outs for larger businesses predate 2018; foreign providers moved contracts into the EU

Bank of Cyprus's 2011 edition and Hellenic Bank's 2017 edition withheld the two months' notice from companies that are not micro-enterprises. Dated fee tables show new and higher account charges and, in 2020-2022, charges on euro balances. Between 2019 and 2022 four foreign providers moved their Cyprus contracts out of United Kingdom entities or English law.

Law 31(I)/2018 lets a provider and a user that is not a consumer agree that its information rules and listed protections do not apply, in whole or in part, and agree a time limit other than the 13 months of art. 71 for notifying an unauthorised payment; a micro-enterprise is treated like a consumer (arts 38 and 61, the latter as amended by Law 32(I)/2019). In outline, assembled from the terms the banks published on 4 October 2026, all three large banks use this against a company that is not a micro-enterprise. The dated editions below show how far back the editions read carry such clauses.169172173183184186187

Question 3 · Entry points

Entry points: banks hold the accounts; resident card acquirers are payment and e-money institutions

On 4 October 2026 the Central Bank of Cyprus (CBC) register lists four locally authorised credit institutions and three subsidiaries of EU banks. Among resident providers, per a CBC release, only payment and e-money institutions acquire cards; eleven Cyprus-licensed firms, JCC among them, offer it on their sites. Others, banks too, serve Cyprus cross-border.

Banks: the CBC register of credit institutions, read 4 October 2026, lists four locally authorised institutions (Ancoria Bank, Bank of Cyprus, Cyprus Development Bank, Housing Finance Corporation), three subsidiaries of EU banks (Alpha Bank Cyprus, Eurobank Limited, National Bank of Greece (Cyprus)), one subsidiary of a non-EU bank, three branches of EU banks and four branches of non-EU banks.332

What happened to the bank list

  • 2015: FBME Bank's licence to operate a branch in Cyprus was revoked as of 21 December.334
  • 2018: Cyprus Cooperative Bank surrendered its licence on 3 September, when the sale of certain assets and liabilities to Hellenic Bank was effectively completed.335
  • 2022: the European Central Bank (ECB) announced on 22 December that it had withdrawn RCB Bank's licence after a voluntary phase-out.336
  • 2025: the assets and liabilities of Eurobank Cyprus were transferred to Hellenic Bank effective 1 September; Hellenic Bank was then renamed Eurobank Limited. The ECB records that Eurobank Cyprus Ltd's licence was withdrawn with effect from 20 September 2025.301337
  • 2025: Alpha Bank Cyprus acquired substantially all of AstroBank's assets and liabilities, effective 31 October per the GLEIF legal-entity record (announced 3 November). AstroBank's licence ended between 31 December 2025 and 1 March 2026 - an inference: the CBC still counted five local authorised institutions at end-2025, and the ECB's list with cut-off 1 March 2026 no longer names it; the exact date was not found.303338339

Who acquires: the Central Bank of Cyprus's statistical release 'Payment Statistics: second half of 2025' (published 22 July 2026), built on reports from 'all Cyprus resident payment service providers', says payment institutions and electronic money institutions 'are the exclusive providers of money remittances and card acquiring services in Cyprus' - which implies that no resident credit institution acquires cards. The release backs this with no figures: card acquiring 'is not presented separately nor analyzed in this report'. The sentence is absent from the two previous releases, and it does not cover providers serving Cyprus merchants cross-border.340

Not there look again by 5 Jan 2027

No card-acceptance product of their own was found on the websites of Bank of Cyprus, Eurobank Limited and Alpha Bank Cyprus on 4 October 2026 (business pages, two sitemaps, three fee tables); acquiring sold through branches would not show there. Cyprus Development Bank's 'Merchant Services' page reads 'Connect Your POS With Your Account with cdbbank Through JCC'; Ancoria Bank's business page lists none; National Bank of Greece (Cyprus) has a card-acceptance menu item that gave 'Page not found' (5 October 2026).341342

JCC Payment Systems Ltd is a 75%-owned subsidiary of Bank of Cyprus. The holding 'increased from 45% to 75%' following the acquisition of certain operations of Laiki Bank, and JCC was fully consolidated from 29 March 2013 (prospectus of 30 November 2016); the annual reports opened since show 75%, as does the interim report at 30 June 2026. On 12 November 2024 the bank disclosed a strategic review 'which may result in a potential disposal of part or all of its holding in JCC'; its Annual Financial Report 2024 says the Board concluded that 'there is greater value to stakeholders through retaining JCC as part of the Group'.343344345346347

Wallets: Apple Pay and Google Pay come through the card-acceptance contract

  • Visa's public rules (edition 18 April 2026) put wallets that hand the card credential to the merchant in the class 'Pass-Through Digital Wallet': the merchant 'finalizes the Transaction with its Acquirer'; Visa names no wallet brand. Mastercard's Rule 9.2.2 (edition 2 June 2026) forbids a pass-through operator to charge a merchant 'any fee or other charge for the acceptance of Mastercard Account credentials'.403404
  • Apple's page (read 4 October 2026) tells a business that already accepts cards to 'contact your payment provider'; no Apple contract was found for a shop terminal, and its terms for websites enabled through a platform (updated 10 March 2023) set no fee payable to Apple. Google's Pay API Terms of Service (effective 1 March 2021) bind an online merchant to Google LLC and leave the acquiring agreement to the merchant.405406
  • Providers serving Cyprus that state wallet acceptance, pages read 4 October 2026: myPOS ('Google Pay and Apple Pay using our diverse range of card machines'), payabl. (Google Pay, Apple Pay and Samsung Pay), SumUp's Cyprus page (Apple Pay and Google Pay), DECTA (Apple Pay). Stripe's Apple Pay guide says it handles Apple merchant validation and that 'you pay only the Stripe processing fees'.407

EU sanctions limit whom a Cyprus bank or acquirer may serve (text consolidated 24 July 2026). Since 24 October 2025 art. 5b(2) of Regulation (EU) No 833/2014, in the wording of Regulation (EU) 2025/2033, prohibits acquiring of payment transactions and issuing of payment instruments or e-money for Russian nationals, natural persons residing in Russia and entities established there; art. 5b(1) prohibits accepting deposits from them, or from non-EU entities more than 50% owned by them, if total deposits per credit institution exceed EUR 100,000. Nationals of, and residence-permit holders in, an EU or EEA state or Switzerland are exempt (art. 5b(3)). More under founders from outside Cyprus.408409410

Question 3, continued · The market in numbers

The market in numbers, 2012-2026: fewer banks, more payment firms, volumes mostly abroad

Register entries of credit institutions fell from 57 (November 2015) to 18 (June 2025). Official totals of payment and e-money institutions disagree. Cyprus-resident providers acquired 1,576 million card payments in 2025 (second half provisional), 77% at points of sale abroad. Non-residents' share of deposits fell from 38.3% in 2012 to 11.9% in August 2026.

Why the totals differ, as far as the records explain it: the Payment Statistics releases draw on the ECB payments-statistics collection (Regulation ECB/2013/43) - their totals equal the sums of the ECB's two series for Cyprus, revised between releases (end-2024: 38, then 34) - while the annual reports count licences. The ECB's split between EMIs and PIs is the reverse of the annual reports'. Neither says who is counted. The Annual Report 2025 gives 28 EMIs that 'were operating' at year-end, though its own flows (26 at end-2024, 4 licensed and 1 withdrawn in 2025) give 29; it does not say which institution it leaves out.420422423

  • The CBC annual reports for 2015-2023, read one by one on 4 October 2026, contain no table or stock count of licensed institutions. They give banks in TARGET2-CY - 22 (18 direct, 4 indirect) in the 2015 report, 21 (17 + 4) in 2016 and 2017, 19 (16 + 3) in 2018 - and flows across all licence types, with no breakdown: 'fifteen institutions' licensed in 2022 and 'nine entities' in 2023.421
  • Two firms are in both registers: Payabl. Cy Limited and Paycomcy Limited are listed as PIs and, licensed 4 January 2024 and 24 June 2026, as EMIs, each with a note that it keeps its payment-institution licence until the e-money licence 'gets activated'. The 32 EMI and 10 PI rows are therefore 40 legal entities; with the one account-information service provider, 41 distinct licensed entities.350426

How much of the acquired volume is abroad

  • By point of sale, 2025 (second half provisional): of 1,576 million payments worth EUR 63.8 billion, 369 million and EUR 20.1 billion were initiated at points of sale in Cyprus and 1,207 million and EUR 43.7 billion abroad - 77% by number, 68% by value; of those abroad, 903 million and EUR 31.0 billion in other EEA countries, 304 million and EUR 12.7 billion outside the EEA.431
  • In 2022 the share abroad by point of sale was 79% by number and 62% by value. Acquirers passported into Cyprus are not in these figures.431
  • By card issuer: in the second half of 2025 (provisional), 763 of 848 million acquired payments and EUR 29.0 of 33.0 billion were cross-border, i.e. the card issuer is outside Cyprus; domestic in 2025: 162 million, EUR 7.8 billion. That split is by issuer, not merchant. Acquired payments are about six times the number made with Cyprus-issued cards (251 million in 2025).430

CY, Solid Processing, Sureswipe and TFI Ecommpay). It gives only BIC and name and does not say who is a direct participant. As of 4 October 2026 the CBC's list of participants in T2-CY, the Cyprus component of T2, names no payment or e-money institution, a year after K.D.P. 293/2025 made their admission possible; the page is undated and lists no account holders, so it does not show whether any has been admitted.442443

The bank account register and the shell-company clean-up: what is dated and what is counted

  • The Central Register of Bank Accounts, Payment Accounts and Safe Deposit Boxes was built before the law that names it: the CBC's Annual Report 2019 lists it among systems developed during 2019, and its statutory basis, art. 61Δ of Law 188(I)/2007, came with Law 13(I)/2021 on 23 February 2021. No CBC announcement of a go-live date was found (4 October 2026).444445
  • Per a software vendor's posts of 5 November and 2 December 2019 (press-class, one source, unconfirmed by the CBC), testing of the register was planned for the last week of November 2019 and go-live was then 'planned for the next two weeks'; that it happened then is not shown.446
  • Direct access to the register: MOKAS, the Police, the Tax and Customs Departments and, from 25 July 2025, the National Sanctions Implementation Unit. The CBC records every access and deletes entries after five years unless an audit is under way. Art. 61Δ is silent on telling the account holder that the register was searched; for the Unit, Law 150(I)/2025 rules out notifying the holder.447448
  • Shell companies: the CBC stated on 16 November 2023 that from the end of 2018 until then credit institutions had terminated relationships with 42,728 shell companies and closed 125,782 bank accounts. The statement gives no method, period breakdown or definition for the two counts.449
  • MONEYVAL's report adopted in December 2019 gives no count of closed accounts. It records that total assets of Cypriot banks fell from EUR 122.9 billion in 2012 to EUR 60.5 billion in 2018 and banks' reliance on introducers from 1,880 business relationships in 2014 to 1,015 in 2018, and that authorities estimated 20 to 30% of Cyprus-registered legal persons to be owned or controlled by non-residents.450
  • That estimate was built on CBC figures for non-resident beneficial owners' share of deposits; it leaves out companies banking abroad and is, the report says, 'likely to be higher'.450
Not there look again by 5 Jan 2027

No official count of the shell-company closures of 2018-2020 was found beyond the CBC total of 16 November 2023, which has no yearly breakdown and no counting method (as of 4 October 2026): the CBC annual reports for 2018, 2019 and 2020 do not contain the word 'shell'.451

Not there look again by 5 Jan 2027

Not published in the ECB data read on 4-5 October 2026: volumes of the JCC Cards system for 2013 and from 2022; the number of payments with Cyprus-issued cards for 2018-2020; terminals located in Cyprus for 2014-2016 and 2019-2025. Bank of Cyprus's annual reports for 2022 to 2025 count no JCC merchants, terminals or transactions.348427429433

Question 4 · An online business and an offline business

Online shop: online contract and published prices. Café: a card duty and JCC's unpublished price

Both walk-throughs are outlines assembled from records. Selling online as such needs no licence; the shop accepts Stripe's agreement online. The café needs a catering licence, unless excluded, and municipal licences inside a municipality, must accept cards under a 2021 decree and chooses JCC's individually priced agreement or a provider's published tariff.

(i) Online shop run by a Cyprus company, cards through Stripe: outline assembled from the records

  1. Incorporate and registerTax Register within 60 days; beneficial owners within 90 days
    An advocate drafts the memorandum and articles; after name approval the company files forms HE1, HE2 and HE3 with the Registrar of Companies (€165 in total with share capital, as of 4 October 2026), files its beneficial owners and obtains a tax identification number. VAT registration is compulsory once taxable supplies exceed €15,600 in 12 months.6781220453
  2. Payout account
    The company needs an account with an IBAN for payouts. Bank of Cyprus's first-account checklist is in the KYC table; its online form says an officer contacts the applicant 'within 3 business days', then a branch meeting completes the opening.24377454
  3. Contract
    The company accepts the Stripe Services Agreement online; nothing is signed on paper. The contracting entity is Stripe Payments Europe, Limited; Stripe Technology Europe, Limited, an Irish electronic money institution (EMI) passported to Cyprus, provides the regulated financial services and acts as payment method acquirer. For a Cyprus user the agreement (General Terms last modified 28 September 2026) is governed by the laws of Ireland, with ICC arbitration in Dublin; Cyprus is not named.219220221454
  4. Data and documents
    Per Stripe's Connect requirements tool (a proxy: Stripe publishes no field list for direct accounts), it enters company name, address, tax ID, category code, website, product description, a representative, every director and owner, and the payout IBAN. If Stripe asks for proof, it uploads from Stripe's Cyprus list: certificate of incorporation or articles, passport or ID card, a utility bill or bank statement, an ownership document such as the beneficial-owner register extract.454455456457
  5. Risk checks and first payoutinitial settlement timing 7 calendar days; default 3 business days
    The business must be outside Stripe's prohibited list (representative, not exhaustive). Stripe's documentation gives Cyprus an initial settlement timing of 7 calendar days for the first payout, typically scheduled to complete within 7–14 days after the first live payment, and a default of 3 business days for later payouts; risk criteria may keep an account off the default timing. Stripe may impose a reserve by notice and publishes no standard reserve percentage or holding period (checked 4 October 2026).239240242456
  6. Tariffas published on 4 October 2026
    Per online card payment: 1.5% + €0.25 for a standard EEA card, 2.8% + €0.25 premium EEA, 2.5% + €0.25 UK, 3.15% + €0.25 international, plus 2% when currency conversion is required; no setup or monthly fees. A dispute costs €20.00, and a further €20.00 if answered manually, returned only if the dispute is won.241382458
  7. Income tax and yearly filingsprovisional tax: 31 July and 31 December
    Outline, a list not a computation: corporate income tax 15% from 1 January 2026 (12.5% before); provisional tax instalments dated 31 July and 31 December; for tax years from 2026, return by 31 January of the second following year where accounts are audited or reviewed. The audited or reviewed financial statements accompany the annual return to the Registrar.52555778459460
  8. VAT and data reportingquarterly VAT returns
    Outline: sales to consumers in other Member States are taxed in Cyprus up to EUR 10,000 a year EU-wide, above that at the customer's Member State rate, optionally through the One Stop Shop; the merchant's payment service provider reports it under CESOP above 25 cross-border payments to the same payee in a calendar quarter. Stripe says it supplies its services from Ireland and does not charge VAT on its fees except to account holders in listed jurisdictions; Cyprus is not listed (read 4 October 2026).461462463464465
  9. VAT on the provider's fee
    Services bought from a provider outside Cyprus fall under the reverse charge of art. 11 of VAT Law 95(I)/2000; an exempt financial service bears none (art. 11(5)). Processing, clearing and authorisation 'in relation to credit cards' have been outside the exemption since 2006; debit cards are not named. A reading, not a ruling: if the fee is such a service, the merchant self-accounts at 19% (return boxes 1 and 4). No Tax Department circular on a merchant service charge was found on 4 October 2026.466467468469470471

(i) Online shop beyond the company: no licence aimed at selling online as such; duties toward the consumer and their 2026 amendments

SubjectInstrument and statusThe ruleDetails; limits of the source
Licence for selling online; the disclosure the Law requiresElectronic Commerce Law 156(I)/2004 (amended by Law 97(I)/2007), ss. 7(1) and 8; in force on 5 October 2026.Cyprus has no licence aimed at selling online as such. Under s. 7(1) taking up and pursuing the activity of an information-society service provider is not subject to prior authorisation or any requirement of equivalent effect, without prejudice to authorisation schemes not aimed specifically at such services.The Law requires disclosure (s. 8(1)): name, geographic address, contact details including e-mail, register and registration number, the supervisory authority where the activity needs approval, the VAT number where VAT applies. Distance contracts with consumersThe Consumer Protection Service's page for businesses selling at a distance: undated, footer 2022, read 5 October 2026; it links to the Consumer Protection Law of 2021. The Service enforces Law 112(I)/2021, amended by Laws 30(I), 75(I) and 122(I)/2026; its powers under it were not read beyond the definitions on 4 October 2026.The page lists: pre-contract information (the trader's identity and address, the total price with all charges, the terms of withdrawal); confirmation on a durable medium at the latest on delivery or before the service starts; delivery within 30 days unless agreed otherwise.Also: 14 days to withdraw (from delivery for goods, from the contract for services), up to one year more if the information was not given; refund within 14 days of the notice. The page names no registration and does not reflect the Law's 2026 amendments; the next two rows carry provisions of Laws 30(I) and 122(I)/2026.287474475476
Withdrawal function on the online interfaceSection 22A of the Consumer Protection Law 112(I)/2021, added by Law 30(I)/2026 (Gazette 5080, 23 March 2026), transposing Directive (EU) 2023/2673. It bears the words 'Πατήστε εδώ για υπαναχώρηση' or an equivalent, stays available through the withdrawal period, and is prominent and easy to reach.The consumer gives name, contract and an electronic address and confirms with a control marked 'επιβεβαίωση υπαναχώρησης'; the trader acknowledges on a durable medium without undue delay. Pre-contract information must say that the function exists and where (new s. 17(1)(η), added by the same Law).475
Additions to pre-contract informationLaw 122(I)/2026 (Gazette 5093, 17 July 2026), amending s. 17(1) of the Consumer Protection Law 112(I)/2021 and adding s. 17A, to transpose Directive (EU) 2024/825. A duty since 27 September 2026.A distance seller's pre-contract information must also include a reminder of the legal guarantee of conformity and its main elements, including its minimum two-year duration, shown by the EU 'harmonised notice'.Also: the 'harmonised label' where the producer gives a free durability guarantee of over two years on the whole good and has told the trader; environmentally friendly delivery options where available; and, where the producer supplies it, the minimum period of software updates.476

(ii) Café in Limassol run by a company, through JCC and through a web-onboarded provider: outline assembled from the records

  1. Card-acceptance dutyone month from starting the activity
    Restaurants and bars are among the listed activities that must accept card payments from consumers (art. 30A of Law 4/1978 and Decree K.D.P. 259/2021, K.D.P. being the Cyprus numbering for regulatory administrative acts; the outline names activity codes 56.10 and 56.30). Any acceptance device counts, including mobile and virtual point-of-sale (POS) terminals; four-party scheme cards must be accepted, through a lawfully licensed payment service provider or its agent. The fine is up to €6,000 from 1 January 2026.28277278289477
  2. JCC: application
    The company holds a current bank account, mandatory on JCC's form. It fills in the form (registration, tax identification and VAT numbers, expected annual card turnover, average transaction value), signs and stamps it and emails it with the KYC documents, 13 items for a company 'as applicable', to JCC, a Cyprus-licensed electronic money institution 75% owned by Bank of Cyprus at 30 June 2026, a holding the bank has had since 29 March 2013.27222344345478479
  3. JCC: contract, price, settlement, terminal
    The individual 'Agreement for the Participation in Card Schemes' takes effect when signed by the merchant and accepted by JCC in writing; either party may end it on 15 days' written notice (in Version 2.8 of 2023 and later; up to Version 1.3 of January 2015 JCC had to give two months). It sets the merchant service charge, the payment timing and any rolling reserve or bank guarantee. A once-off €17 registration fee is debited from the account. A POS rented from JCC may be programmed only by JCC-authorised agents.27224237264288327480
  4. Web-onboarded provider: sign-up
    The same café signs up online with myPOS (an Irish EMI), Viva (a Greek bank) or SumUp (a Lithuanian EMI); none is Cyprus-licensed. myPOS emails a document list and says verification usually completes within 72 business hours; Viva says it mostly retrieves company data from the business registry and asks for a valid ID, and more may be requested. myPOS's agreement is accepted by click under Irish law, SumUp's General Terms by ticking a box under the law of Lithuania; Viva's terms are governed by the laws of Greece.225226227228229230245388481
  5. Web-onboarded provider: terminal, tariff, settlementas published on 4 October 2026
    In-person rates are in the chart. SumUp readers cost €34, €139 and €169 excluding 19% VAT; Revolut terminals €189 or €139 plus VAT, with a Business plan from €10 a month (its FAQ excludes sole traders, its terms admit them). Viva's 'Zero' plan has a €4.99 minimum monthly charge. myPOS and Viva credit takings at once to their own account; a SEPA transfer out costs €4.00 at myPOS, €0.80 at Viva. Revolut advertises next-day payout; SumUp's price page says 'the next business day', its help article 2-3 business days.231243248252390391393482
  6. VATquarterly returns
    Outline: 9%, the rate for restaurant and catering services, on food and drink supplied with support services for immediate consumption; without them the supply counts as foodstuffs at 5%, except alcoholic drinks, beer, wine and soft drinks at 19%. Registration above €15,600. Under Decree K.D.P. 354/2026, as announced by the Tax Department on 2 October 2026, coffee bought as beans, ground or instant is zero-rated from 12 October 2026 to 31 May 2027; ready-made coffee drinks are excluded.12463477483484485
  7. Payrollcontributions due by the end of the following month
    The employer applies to register with the Social Insurance Services (form YKA 1-001) at least a day before becoming an employer and declares each hiring electronically at least a day ahead (since 13 September 2021). On 4 October 2026: social insurance 8.8% each from employee and employer on earnings up to €5,742 a month; General Healthcare System (GeSY) 2.65% and 2.90%; employer-only Redundancy Fund 1.2%, Human Resource Development levy 0.5% and Social Cohesion Fund 2%, the last on total earnings without ceiling.151617486487488489
  8. Receiptsat the time of each sale
    A VAT-registered café issues and delivers to every consumer a 'legal receipt' at the time of sale (reg. 13A of the VAT (General) Regulations K.D.P. 314/2001, applied from 16 January 2012), showing among other things its name, address and VAT number. A taxable customer may ask for an invoice; up to €85 a simplified one suffices if the customer is not in another Member State (reg. 14). VAT is due on the full price charged, not on the amount settled after the merchant service charge (Court of Justice, C-18/92).490491492
  9. Inspections and penalties
    Cards: per Tax Department Implementing Directive 20/2021 a terminal stands 'at all tills without exception'; a breach is reported within five working days, the fine decided within fifteen, objection within 30 days (Law 4/1978, art. 50ΣΤ). Receipts (VAT Law, arts 45(9), 46(11A)): a charge of 20% of the transaction value; on conviction a fine of up to €1,700, up to three years in prison, or both. Since 1 January 2026: sealing for up to ten days after three notices (art. 32A of Law 4/1978), not for refusing cards.493494495496497

(ii) Café beyond the company: catering licence, municipal licences, manager, sanitary and food-handler certificates (texts read on 5 October 2026)

Licence or certificateInstrument and issuerWhat it asksValidity, times as published, where the texts differ
Catering establishment licenceCatering Establishments Law 29/1985, s. 6(1): a restaurant, taverna, cafeteria, bar or similar place serving food or drink for payment may not operate without a licence. It is issued by the Deputy Ministry of Tourism (Law 123(I)/2018).A sanitary certificate and the fee (s. 6(3)). Section 2 excludes traditional coffee-shops ('καφενεία'), take-away-only shops, certain canteens, and shops with a service area under 8 m² serving no alcohol.Since Law 170(I)/2020 the licence expires every three years; the government business portal (18 September 2026) still says one year, to 31 December. The portal also says to apply at least one month before opening, with a decision within three months.498
The procedure for that licenceThe Deputy Ministry of Tourism's procedure sheet for a catering licence (dated December 2018, posted 28 May 2024, read 5 October 2026); it has five stages.(A) planning permission, sought by the owner; (B) approval of the plans by the Deputy Ministry (form F-KEN-01/1); (C) a building or change-of-use permit; (D) after the works, verification by district inspectors and filing of forms F-KEN-02/1 and F-KEN-05/1, even while the permit is pending; (E) classification and the licence.Stage (E) is on conditions that include a copy of the permit, a sanitary certificate and the fee. For stage (C) the sheet names the municipality or District Officer; that is now the District Local Government Organisation (Law 37(I)/2022, s. 20(2)(β)).499
Manager of the establishmentLaw 29/1985, s. 16 (read 5 October 2026): a licensed catering establishment must have a manager who meets statutory conditions, and the owner may fill the post only if he meets them.The manager must be a graduate of a recognised hotel or tourism school with knowledge of food and drink, or hold a secondary-school leaving certificate and one year's catering experience, or have at least three years' experience judged satisfactory by the licensing authority.For class A and B establishments only the school route counts. The manager must also be of good character, shown by a Chief of Police certificate of no conviction for listed offences. The Law sets no nationality condition for the manager.500
Municipal licences, inside a municipality, beside the tourism licenceMunicipalities Law 52(I)/2022. Section 55(1)(γ): a prior municipal licence for premises over 50 m² used as a restaurant, taverna, snack bar, cafeteria or pizzeria. Section 56(1), the licence for any business premises, excepts those cases and so covers smaller ones. Section 44(1) adds sound-emission and alcohol licences.The s. 55(1)(γ) licence is given on a building permit and engineer's, electrical, fire and municipal-health certificates.The s. 55(1)(γ) licence is for up to three years. Under Cap. 144, s. 11, an alcohol licence expires on 12 March. The business portal, still citing the 1985 Municipalities Law, gives four months for the premises decision and two for alcohol (premises page modified 22 October 2020, alcohol page updated 7 December 2023).501
Sanitary certificateLaw 29/1985, s. 2, defines it as the certificate issued by the Health Service of the Ministry of Health or by a municipal health service, as the case may be. The Municipalities Law 52(I)/2022, s. 55(2)(ε), requires a municipal health service certificate for the municipal licence of premises over 50 m².Who issues the certificate depends on the licence. The business portal's alcohol-licence list also asks, where applicable, for the tourism licence and a criminal record certificate under 3 months old.The business portal follows unevenly: its catering page (18 September 2026) names the Ministry's services, its alcohol-licence page (7 December 2023) and its premises page the municipality.502
Health Certificate for Food Handlers; registration of the establishmentPer the government business portal (updated 2 May 2024), staff who handle unpacked food in a food business need the certificate from a Chief Medical Officer of the Ministry of Health. Law 29/1985, s. 17(2): in a licensed catering establishment every person employed must hold a sanitary certificate.Per the portal there is no application form: a stool sample is tested for salmonella and parasites at the person's own cost, then the officer issues the certificate the same day for €22 plus a registration fee.Per the portal the certificate is valid twelve months. Source trap

The card-acceptance decree obliges payees whose main activity code is in its Annex. The Annex lists store retail codes 47.11–47.78 but not 47.91 (mail-order and internet retail); the amending decrees K.D.P. 446/2021, 52/2022 and 248/2022 added eight codes, none of them 47.91 (read 4 October 2026). A Cyprus merchant may not surcharge card payments. JCC's Terms v2.10 record that 'in accordance with applicable law, the application of any Surcharge is prohibited' (clause 2.2). Under Law 31(I)/2018 no charge is allowed for instruments with interchange fees capped under Regulation (EU) 2015/751 (art. 62(4)), and a payee may not request charges for using a specific payment instrument (art. 62(5)); per a House committee report of 23 May 2023 the Ministry of Finance read it as 'the universal prohibition, without exceptions'. The Consumer Protection Service may fine a payee up to €2,000 (art. 99B); no case applying the ban was found in its 2022-2026 decision lists or on CyLaw (5 October 2026).271272286288513514

Question 5 · Laws, rules and supervisors

The Central Bank supervises providers; merchants' card duties sit with tax and consumer bodies

The Central Bank of Cyprus supervises credit, payment and e-money institutions and is their anti-money-laundering (AML) supervisor; the European Central Bank supervises significant banks prudentially. The Tax Department enforces the card-acceptance duty, the Consumer Protection Service the surcharge rules. Card schemes set an acquirer's checks on a merchant.

The surcharge ban and how it is policed

  • Three paragraphs of art. 62 of Law 31(I)/2018 bear on a payee's charges. Paragraph (3) reproduces PSD2's cost-based allowance. Paragraph (4) never allows a charge for instruments whose interchange is capped under Regulation (EU) 2015/751. Paragraph (5), unchanged since 18 April 2018, adds without qualification that a payee may not request charges for the use of a specific payment instrument.271286
  • Law 36(I)/2023 (Official Gazette No. 4947, 2 June 2023) replaced the opening word of art. 60(1), 'Where', with 'Subject to paragraph (5) of Article 62, where'. Since then the duty to tell the payer in advance about a charge or discount for a given payment instrument is expressly subordinate to the ban.570
  • The Government reads paragraph (5) as a ban with no exceptions: the House Finance and Budget Committee's report of 23 May 2023 records the Ministry of Finance explaining that 'the legislator's intention was the universal prohibition, without exceptions' of such charges. That commercial and three-party cards are covered is an inference from 'without exceptions', not the report's words.272
  • The Consumer Protection Service polices the ban under powers added by Law 16(I)/2022: it may demand information from a payee, inspect its premises and order it to stop an infringement at once (art. 99A) and, after hearing the payee, impose an administrative fine of up to EUR 2,000 and, if the infringement continues, up to EUR 100 a day (art. 99B). Giving the Service false information is a criminal offence.513
Not there look again by 5 Apr 2027

No published decision or judgment applying the surcharge ban was found on 5 October 2026. The Consumer Protection Service's 2022-2026 decision lists hold 94 entries; of the 15 fines at or under EUR 2,000, the cap for a surcharge fine, nine were opened and six share the price-monitoring code — all under other laws. CyLaw's search of Cypriot judgments returns none on a surcharge. No Commission or EBA answer on surcharging commercial or three-party cards was found in the Commission's PSD2 FAQ or the EBA Q&A tool.514571

The card-acceptance duty: how it is applied and enforced

PointAs the records state it
Scope, in the Tax Department's readingImplementing Directive 20/2021 (4 August 2021): every payee whose activity is in the decree's Annex must accept cards 'regardless of the amount of the payment, the turnover of the business and regardless of whether it is registered or obliged to register in the VAT Register', with a terminal 'at all tills without exception'.493
Procedure for the fineArt. 50ΣΤ of Law 4/1978 (read 5 October 2026): the officer reports the breach to the Tax Commissioner within five working days; the fine is imposed within fifteen working days of the report; an objection may be made within 30 days of notification and is decided within 30 days; that decision can go to the Administrative Court.494
InspectionsThe Tax Department's announcement of 3 May 2023: continuous checks, every complaint examined, penalties imposed 'without necessarily publicising the results or its actions'. No card-specific count of inspections or fines was found by 5 October 2026. Refusing cards is no ground for sealing a business under art. 32A of Law 4/1978.495572
No technical linkOn 5 October 2026 no rule in force or government announcement was found linking cash registers or card terminals electronically to the tax administration. Cash registers are 'fiscal electronic devices' (K.D.P. 29/97, 224/2010); the latter's contents name fiscal memory, sealing, licensing, not data transmission (read in part).573574
The only official text found that spoke of a link: the recovery-plan annex (Council Implementing Decision)In the annex of 28 July 2021, and still as amended on 20 June 2025, the Tax Department's new IT system was to include 'connecting businesses to a server held within the Tax Department, without the use of specialised mechanisms'. The amendment of 12 December 2025 cut the line. Cash registers and card terminals were never named.575

Deposit guarantee: client accounts and electronic money

PointAs the records state it
Look-throughWhere the depositor is not absolutely entitled to the sums in an account, the guarantee covers the person who is, provided that person's identity is or can be established before the deposit becomes unavailable; where several are entitled, each one's share counts towards the EUR 100,000 limit (reg. 10(e) of K.D.P. 27/2016).537
Client account (K.D.P. 84/2020, 6 March 2020)An account held on behalf of persons, other than those in whose name it is held, who are its absolute beneficiaries. Its holder must keep accurate and up-to-date information on them, including their identity, and give it to the credit institution and/or the scheme's Management Committee within seven working days of a request.576
Same person, same bankPer the CBC's deposit-guarantee FAQ (file dated 8 October 2025, q.24): a beneficiary's share in a client account and his or her personal deposit at the same bank 'are summed up', the total being capped at EUR 100,000. The FAQ does not name safeguarding accounts of payment or e-money institutions.577578
Electronic moneyArt. 3(2) of Law 5(I)/2016 (consolidated text to Law 119(I)/2021, read 4 October 2026): amounts defined as electronic money under the Electronic Money Law do not fall within the scope of the Law; art. 3(1) applies it to credit institutions. The Law has no rule on client or beneficiary accounts; those sit in the Regulations.538
Open look again by 11 May 2028

On 4 October 2026 the texts do not settle whether the deposit guarantee covers customers of a payment or e-money institution whose safeguarding account is at a Cyprus bank (outline assembled from the records): the regulations define a 'client account' regardless of who holds it, which fits a payment institution's segregated account; art. 3(2) of Law 5(I)/2016 puts electronic money outside the scheme; no Cyprus text names safeguarding accounts. The express EU rule, Directive (EU) 2026/804, applies from 11 May 2028.552578579

The central register of bank accounts

  • Art. 61Δ of Law 188(I)/2007, inserted by Law 13(I)/2021 (23 February 2021), creates a Central Register of Bank Accounts, Payment Accounts and Safe Deposit Boxes kept by the CBC. Supervised institutions supply the identification data of the holder, of any person acting for the holder and of the beneficial owner, the IBAN and the dates of opening and closing.445
  • As enacted, MOKAS and the Police had direct access for their tasks under the AML Law, the Tax and Customs Departments to investigate and prosecute art. 3 offences. Since Law 40(I)/2022 (30 March 2022) the four may search to prevent, detect, investigate or prosecute a prescribed offence or trace assets, by specially authorised staff only. The National Sanctions Implementation Unit has access from 25 July 2025.447
  • Art. 61Δ is silent on telling an account holder of a search: no duty to notify, no 'without notification' clause; for the National Sanctions Implementation Unit, Law 150(I)/2025 s. 18(d) rules notification out. The CBC logs every access and deletes entries after five years unless an audit is under way. Its Annual Report 2019 lists the register as developed in 2019; no go-live announcement was found (4 October 2026).444448

Risk categories, monitoring thresholds, dispute time limits, PCI questionnaires and interchange tables are set out in the section on the card schemes.

PCI DSS v4.0.1, published on 11 June 2024, is the only active version since v4.0 was retired on 31 December 2024; no later version was found on 4 October 2026.
